papers.field: Protein-structure distillation workflows and scientific machine-learning inference
papers.summary: ElMerFold optimizes an OpenFold 2-based workflow that generates protein structures for OpenFold 3 training. It combines FP32 inference kernels and a C++ runtime with persistent inference servers, resource-aware task scheduling, staged near-node storage and fault recovery. These changes overlap model execution, template searches, relaxation and data movement across El Capitan.

machine_configurations.name: El Capitan
machine_configurations.configuration: 11,520 nodes total, each with four AMD MI300A APUs and 512 GiB coherent HBM3 shared by CPU/GPU dies; no separate DRAM. Each APU has three 8-core Zen 4 CCDs and six 38-CU CDNA3 XCDs. Nodes use HPE Slingshot. Merced is a 401 PiB HDD Lustre capacity tier. 720 Rabbit near-node-storage modules each have sixteen 2 TiB NVMe SR-IOV drives and connect to sixteen compute nodes; this workflow stages static data into a 500 GiB shared read-only XFS area and gives each node a 600 GiB private XFS area. Largest run uses 11,200 nodes/44,800 APUs, reserving at most eleven critical nodes for Flux rather than application work.
machine_configurations.location: PDF p. 7, section VI-B and Figure 4; PDF p. 6, sections V-C/D

measurements.precision: FP32 model inference. Relaxation uses an FP64 energy/gradient evaluator; its arithmetic is not in the reported inference FLOP numerator. TF32 GEMM and BF16-emulated FP32 experiments were rejected and are not the reported path. No FP64-equivalent conversion.
measurements.scope: Sustained completed-and-written protein structures per second over the six-hour workflow, including startup and I/O
measurements.scale: 11,200 El Capitan nodes, 44,800 AMD MI300A APUs, six-hour workflow run; OpenFold 3 monomer distillation inputs from approximately 41 million MGnify sequences with precomputed MSAs. Up to two predicted structures per sequence, using OpenFold 2 model 1 with templates and model 3 without templates.
measurements.location: PDF p. 9, section VII-C and Figure 7; metric/counting definitions PDF p. 7, section VI and Table II; precision PDF pp. 4 and 10
measurements.measurement_method: Count successfully predicted structures written to Lustre divided by workflow elapsed time. Figure 7 and section VII-C report throughput for the six-hour run. Startup includes Rabbit configuration, launch, data staging and unpacking; approximately 20 minutes elapse before the first structure output.

notes: This is a separate complete-manuscript audit of the LLNL public binary retrieved November 22, 2026. Its PDF build metadata date is not promoted to a source revision date or benchmark measurement date.

No DOI is printed in the manuscript. The DOI is inherited from the exact-title existing IEEE publisher record. Previously recorded doi.org 404/resolver status is not rechecked, erased or overridden by this fulltext audit.

The printed twelve-author order includes Pier Fiedorowicz in position 3. It matches the current November 22 publisher byline, while the preserved November 12 publisher snapshot has eleven authors and omits Fiedorowicz. Those are distinct source versions and the original roster arrays are unchanged.
The 1.807 figure-mean and 1.81 textual sustained rate are the same rounded observation; 1.990 and 1.99 peak are likewise one observation. They must not be counted twice.

Inference uses FP32; the relaxation evaluator uses FP64. TF32 changed predicted structures and BF16 emulation used too much memory without useful speedup, so neither lower-precision experiment is substituted for these observations.

Section VI defines inference FLOP/s using only model-inference operations. Sustained timing includes whole-workflow startup and I/O; that denominator does not turn the numerator into total application FLOPs.

The manuscript reports a 45.4× speedup against an extrapolated baseline, measured only up to 512 nodes and assumed to scale perfectly to 11,200 nodes. This is not added as a directly measured same-scale comparison. The 15.2× single-node inference/relaxation speedup and the LLNL project page’s 17× inference-pipeline statement have different scopes and remain separate.

The precomputed MSAs total about 1.6 PiB uncompressed/260 TiB compressed. They are read by the timed workflow; their initial computation is outside it. Model training and offline tuning are also outside the timing.

Approximately 41 million sequences define the distillation input corpus. The paper does not provide a unique-input count for the six-hour benchmark, so structures/second is not multiplied by time to assert a unique-protein count or dataset completion time.

Existing November 12 snapshot, November 22 postconference metadata and separate ElMerFold performance-history events are preserved. This audit supplies manuscript evidence only and establishes no conference-final score or new award designation.

papers.title: Real-time Bayesian inference at extreme scale: A digital twin for tsunami early warning applied to the Cascadia subduction zone
papers.field: Computational geophysics; Bayesian inverse problems; real-time tsunami forecasting
papers.summary: The authors combine seafloor-pressure observations with a three-dimensional acoustic-gravity model to infer earthquake-driven seafloor motion and predict coastal wave heights with uncertainty. Shift invariance and block-Toeplitz algorithms move expensive PDE solves into one-time offline preparation. The resulting online inference takes less than 0.2 seconds on 512 A100 GPUs for a synthetic Cascadia scenario; the offline wave solver separately scales to 55.5 trillion degrees of freedom on El Capitan.

machine_configurations.name: El Capitan
machine_configurations.configuration: As described in this manuscript: HPE Cray EX, 11,136 nodes, four AMD Instinct MI300A APUs per node. Each APU integrates 24 Zen4 CPU cores, a CDNA3 GPU and 128 GB HBM3. HPE Slingshot-200 dragonfly interconnect. Scaling experiments used 85-10,880 nodes / 340-43,520 APUs (called GPUs in the paper).
machine_configurations.location: PDF pp. 7-9, section VI.A, Table II, Fig. 5.

machine_configurations.name: Alps
machine_configurations.configuration: As described in this manuscript: HPE Cray EX, 2,688 nodes, four NVIDIA GH200 superchips per node; each has a 72-core Grace CPU and H100 GPU with 96 GB HBM3. Slingshot-11 dragonfly interconnect. Scaling run: 36-2,304 nodes / 144-9,216 GPUs.
machine_configurations.location: PDF pp. 7-9, section VI.A, Table II, Fig. 5.

machine_configurations.facility: National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC)
machine_configurations.configuration: As described in this manuscript: HPE Cray Shasta, 1,536 GPU nodes, AMD EPYC 7763 64-core CPU and four NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 40 GB HBM2 per node; Slingshot-11 dragonfly. Time-to-solution experiment uses 128 nodes / 512 GPUs; scaling experiments use 47-1,504 nodes / 188-6,016 GPUs.
machine_configurations.location: PDF pp. 7-10, section VI.A, Table II, Fig. 5, Table III.

measurements.precision: Double precision
measurements.scope: Online Phase 4 Bayesian parameter inference: strict upper bound (<0.2 s), excluding offline preparation
measurements.scale: 128 Perlmutter nodes / 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs; 2,416,530 spatial parameter points x 420 temporal steps (~1.015 billion parameters), 252,000 synthetic noisy observations from 600 hypothesized sensors, and 21 forecast locations.
measurements.location: PDF p. 10, section VII.C and Table III (Phase 4); parameter discretization on p. 7.
measurements.measurement_method: Wall time measured using omp_get_wtime after GPU synchronization and MPI_Barrier (section VI.D, p. 8).
measurements.note: The source reports less than 0.2 s, not an exact 0.2 s value. Phase 1 alone requires 621 independent PDE solutions totaling about 538 hours on 512 GPUs; later offline phases also precede the online result. Table III separately lists QoI-only prediction at <1 ms on one GPU. Synthetic noisy data, not an operational sensor-to-alert deployment benchmark.

measurements.precision: Double precision
measurements.scope: Weak parallel efficiency of the offline acoustic-gravity PDE solver
measurements.scale: 85 to 10,880 nodes / 340 to 43,520 AMD MI300A GPUs; 128-fold increase in GPUs and problem size; largest problem >55.5 trillion DOF (~1.28 billion DOF/APU), using 4.8 PB of memory.
measurements.location: PDF pp. 8-9, section VII.A, Table II and Fig. 5 (left).
measurements.measurement_method: Runtime per RK4 step averaged over ten consecutive time steps (40 operator applications), after discarding the initial ten steps. POSIX wall clocks called after device synchronization and MPI_Barrier (p. 8, section VI.C).
measurements.note: This is an offline-solver scaling efficiency, not the speed or GPU count of the <0.2 s online inference. Table II separates weak-scaling mesh elements from strong-scaling elements per GPU. The distinct strong-scaling test fixes 434 billion DOF and reports 100.9x speedup / 79% efficiency.

measurements.precision: Double precision
measurements.scope: FFT-based Hessian matrix-vector product after precomputing the parameter-to-observation map
measurements.scale: 128 Perlmutter nodes / 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs; 2,416,530 spatial parameter points x 420 temporal steps (~1.015 billion parameters), 252,000 synthetic noisy observations from 600 hypothesized sensors, and 21 forecast locations.
measurements.location: PDF p. 10, section VII.C; Table III form-K row gives 24 ms per matvec.
measurements.measurement_method: Wall timings use omp_get_wtime after device synchronization and MPI_Barrier; vendor FFT/BLAS libraries (section VI.D, p. 8).
measurements.note: Reported as an exact block-Toeplitz Hessian application, without an approximation. The comparison is 104 minutes for a forward/adjoint PDE pair on the same 512 A100 GPUs versus 0.024 s after offline precomputation, yielding the paper's 260,000x speedup. This is not a whole workflow runtime.

papers.title: Ab-initio Quantum Transport with the GW Approximation, 42,240 Atoms, and Sustained Exascale Performance
papers.field: Quantum transport; semiconductor nanodevices; many-body electronic-structure computation
papers.summary: QuaTrEx combines non-equilibrium Green's functions with self-consistent GW electron-interaction calculations to model silicon nanoribbon transistors at experimentally relevant dimensions. A spatial decomposition and recursive Green's-function solver distribute large devices over accelerator ranks. A 42,240-atom case sustains 1,146.037 Pflop/s in FP64 on Frontier, while Alps reaches 342.637 Pflop/s for 46,464 atoms. These are per-iteration application measurements excluding I/O.

papers.field: Distributed machine learning; large language model training
papers.summary: AxoNN combines four dimensions of model and data parallelism to train large transformer models across NVIDIA and AMD supercomputers. Kernel tuning, communication overlap and a performance model reduce training costs while allowing models too large for one accelerator. The paper benchmarks weak scaling on three systems, predicts longer training times from short iteration measurements, and uses the framework to study model memorization and a mitigation through fine-tuning.

papers.title: Breaking the Molecular Dynamics Timescale Barrier Using a Wafer-Scale System
papers.field: Computational materials science; classical molecular dynamics
papers.summary: This work maps each simulated atom to a processor core on a Cerebras wafer-scale engine and uses local dataflow communication to accelerate Embedded Atom Method molecular dynamics. The approach targets the time horizon of a fixed-size simulation, which is limited by communication latency on conventional CPU/GPU clusters. Uniform copper, tungsten and tantalum crystals and a grain-boundary case demonstrate the method; the audited May 2024 version reports measured loop rates for roughly 802,000 atoms and separately models future optimizations and multi-wafer extensions.

papers.title: Massively Parallel 3D Image Reconstruction
papers.field: Computed tomography and model-based iterative image reconstruction
papers.summary: The Non-Uniform Parallel Super-Voxel algorithm accelerates Bayesian model-based iterative CT reconstruction while retaining local coordinate updates. Three-dimensional super-voxels improve cache reuse, block-transposed buffers regularize irregular sinogram accesses for SIMD, and separate parallelism within and between super-voxels and across sub-volumes maps the reconstruction onto a distributed many-core system. Alternating greedy and randomized updates improves convergence. Experiments use materials, biological and security scan data, with reconstruction times and scaling reported separately from comparisons against differently sized baseline implementations.

papers.title: Towards Green Aviation with Python at Petascale
papers.field: High-order computational fluid dynamics and turbine aerodynamics
papers.summary: PyFR uses high-order flux reconstruction to resolve unsteady turbulent flow on curved unstructured meshes. Python coordinates runtime-generated device kernels and vendor matrix multiplication, allowing a single implementation to target different accelerators. The study simulates a loaded low-pressure turbine cascade and compares with experimental surface-flow data. It distinguishes short solver benchmarks without plugins from a longer scientific simulation that includes averaging and checkpoint output.

papers.title: An Extreme-Scale Implicit Solver for Complex PDEs: Highly Heterogeneous Flow in Earth’s Mantle
papers.field: Nonlinear implicit PDE solvers and mantle-flow geodynamics
papers.summary: The solver targets mantle flow with narrow plate boundaries, large viscosity contrasts and nonlinear rheology. Adaptive octree meshes and mixed finite elements reduce the unknown count, while an inexact Newton–Krylov method uses hybrid spectral, geometric and algebraic multigrid with a new Schur-complement preconditioner. Extreme-scale tests measure representative linear-solver iterations; projected complete nonlinear runtimes are explicitly distinguished from those short measurements.

papers.field: Neuromorphic processors and event-driven spiking-network computation
papers.summary: TrueNorth implements a deterministic spiking-network kernel in digital silicon, colocating synaptic memory and neuron updates to reduce data movement. A shared kernel makes networks functionally equivalent to the Compass software simulator, while tiled event-routing supports multichip arrays. Characterization separates synaptic energy efficiency, real-time vision throughput and full-board power. These integer synaptic operations measure a different computational workload from floating-point simulation.

papers.summary: The simulation follows competing dendrites during aluminum–silicon solidification using a phase field and solute-concentration equations on a regular grid. The principal measured interval is the main electronic iteration loop, not a complete long-time FPMD trajectory or entire job including initialization. The 526.91-second metric is per electronic steepest-descent iteration.

Table 2 is a single Gamma-point real-arithmetic strong-scaling series, ending at 64.70 TFlop/s and 55.3 s/iteration. The algorithm performs level-synchronized BFS on distributed undirected graphs. Two-dimensional edge partitioning separates expand and fold phases; fixed message-buffer bounds for Poisson random graphs constrain memory growth. Ring-based collective communication is mapped to the BlueGene/L torus, with set-union during reduce-scatter eliminating duplicate vertices.

Primary scaling studies use synthetic Poisson random graphs, not measured real-world semantic graphs. The paper itself treats clustered and scale-free graphs as future work. Its synthetic graph capacity is not generalized to all graph classes.

The source reports up to roughly 3.2 billion vertices and 32 billion edges. Table 1 specifies local vertex count and average degree, while nearby prose inconsistently refers to some graph sizes as edges. Selected scale therefore retains the unambiguous local vertex/k/topology fields; no reinterpretation of undirected-edge multiplicity or TEPS conversion is made.

Table 1/figures show that 2D layouts reduce communication but do not universally minimize total time for low-degree graphs. The selected 4.800-second 2D result is not presented as the global optimum. Bidirectional-search comparisons and strong-scaling speedups are different experiments, not substituted into this timing.

The system’s theoretical Tflop/s rating describes hardware only. BFS is primarily memory/communication intensive and this audit records a native execution-time metric rather than inventing a floating-point rate. Only one representative timing is selected; all algorithms, plots, tables and references were read.

The code uses second-order central spatial differences and fourth-order Runge-Kutta time integration for compressible rotating MHD. Boundary interpolation joins the panels; radial vectors and horizontal MPI decomposition target the Earth Simulator architecture.

The original performance listing supplies the timing convention: the headline rate is relative to User Time. It is not relabeled as end-to-end elapsed-wall-time throughput merely because Real Time also appears in the same listing. Measurement interval and denominator are retained explicitly.

A separate scientific run uses 3,888 processes and a 255 x 514 x 1538 x 2 grid, taking six wall-clock hours to saturation and saving 127 outputs. It is not paired with the 4,096-process headline. The modeled interval covers only about 0.3% of magnetic free-decay time; repeated field reversals are not claimed as a completed result of that run.

Machine peak, vector-operation ratio and comparisons with earlier Earth Simulator atmosphere/turbulence/fusion/seismic papers have separate definitions and are not additional measured geodynamo throughput observations. notes: Exact title and all nine authors were read on the first page. The preserved proceedings file labels itself Preprint submitted to the 2002 Gordon Bell Award, 15 August 2002. That document date is retained; no final published or conference-day version is authenticated.

Salinas is a C++ implicit finite-element structural-analysis package using 64-bit arithmetic. Its dual-primal FETI-DP method combines domain decomposition, local sparse Cholesky solves, a PCG interface iteration and a coarse correction. Two coarse-solve strategies trade replicated inverse/matrix-vector work against a distributed sparse direct solve; the method is selected by coarse/local problem sizes.

ASCI Red and White headline rates have materially different measurement scopes. Red FLOPs cover the FETI-DP solver only and separate application times exclude I/O; White FLOPs omit no stage and application times include I/O. These distinctions take precedence over broad abstract wording.

The principal scalability experiment is weak scaling: problem size and processor/subdomain count grow together, while each subdomain discretization stays fixed. The optical-shutter experiment separately studies a fixed 16-million-DOF model and a 110-million-DOF case.

There is an internal scale discrepancy for the optical-shutter M2 result: the prose on PDF p. 15 says 3,375 processors, while the preparation description (p. 10) and Table 1/caption (p. 16) say 3,783. The 745 Gflop/s / 418-second M2 result is therefore described as a separate, conflicting-scale case, not silently merged into the selected 3,375-processor cube observation. CPU-efficiency percentages also have minor differences between introductory and detailed wording.

The historical 1999 CFD/spectral-element rates and the peak rates used for efficiency are comparisons, not new Salinas observations. Only two representative achieved rates are selected; all figures, tables and references were read.

notes: Audited source is a complete 13-page author manuscript served by the PETSc-FUN3D project at Argonne, with the exact title and ordered initials above. The PDF has no abstract heading; the English summary here is editorial and is not a reproduced abstract. The author project’s publication list identifies this work as the SC99 paper and links its ICASE 2000-2 report relationship.

The source has no visible issue/revision date or authenticated version history. PDF metadata CreationDate is D:19990925114528, without a timezone; this supports identification of the retrieved file but is not promoted to source_revision_date or measurement_date. The name bell.pdf is not treated as proof of final conference status.

Exact manuscript byline is retained in initials. The author publication list separately expands the names as Kyle Anderson, William D. Gropp, Dinesh K. Kaushik, David E. Keyes and Barry F. Smith; those forms must remain searchable without replacing the verified PDF byline.

Large-scale tests in this manuscript concern the Euler subset. FUN3D also supports Navier-Stokes and a Spalart–Allmaras turbulence model, but the text describes that work on more modest problems and as future scale-up; the reported large-machine headline is not mislabeled as a turbulent Navier-Stokes production run.

The nonlinear method uses pseudo-transient continuation, inexact Newton iteration, a matrix-free Krylov method and an additive Schwarz preconditioner derived from a lower-order, sparser discretization. PETSc provides distributed objects and MPI communication, and MeTiS partitions the mesh. Data interlacing, structural blocking, vertex/edge reordering and communication overlap improve data reuse and parallel execution.

Four selected headline observations are retained, two native metrics for each of two machines. This first pass does not transcribe every point of the scaling figures or every kernel/flow-regime table entry. Tables 1-2 use a separate 357,900-vertex mesh, and Figure 2 uses 22,677 vertices with four unknowns per vertex.

Figure 2 machine-peak and STREAM Triad bars are bounds/comparators for coarse sequential tests. The 235 Mflop/s instruction-scheduling estimate and 209 Mflop/s hardware-counter result in Section 3.2 concern the SGI flux kernel. The historical NWT 111 Gflop/s claim in the conclusion is an attributed prior-work comparison. None is added as a FUN3D large-mesh solver measurement.

ASCI Red topology labels need care: the overview and Section 5.2 explicitly say 2,048 dual-processor nodes, while Section 5’s introduction and Figure 4 caption use processors. The selected scale follows the explicit dual-node description, preserves the runtime-mode distinction and does not infer that both CPUs execute the complete solver.

A separately saved NASA/CR-2000-210080 / ICASE 2000-2 report has a January 2000 cover and reports 3,072 dual-processor nodes, 227 Gflop/s and 15 microseconds per degree of freedom. Only its cover, byline/abstract and overview (PDF pp. 1-3) were checked for this version comparison. Those values are not substituted into the 156 Gflop/s manuscript or added to the selected fully audited observations.

machine_configurations.configuration: TMS320C31-50 DSP nodes with 50 MFLOP/s native 32-bit hardware peak, 60-ns commodity DRAM, and a 250K-transistor custom ASIC with error detection/correction, 32-word programmable cache and eight DMA-controlled bidirectional serial-neighbor connections. 64 nodes form a 4×4×2×2 motherboard array; eight motherboards per backplane; larger four-dimensional torus configurations are cabled from these modules. papers.title: Large Scale Simulation of Suspensions with PVM
papers.field: Suspension rheology and parallel boundary-element simulation
papers.summary: The study models how particles alter a suspension’s resistance to falling and rotating test spheres. A completed double-layer boundary-element formulation avoids storing a large dense system, while asynchronous particle-wise updates distribute the work through PVM. Calculations on a shared AlphaStation farm compare sedimentation and rotational responses across concentrations. The performance analysis uses extrapolated serial-equivalent work and keeps wall-clock throughput separate from CPU-time throughput.

machine_configurations.name: DEC AlphaStation 500/266 workstation farm
machine_configurations.facility: Workstation farm described by the University of Sydney authors; the machine-description section does not explicitly name a room or facility.
machine_configurations.configuration: 28 DEC AlphaStation 500/266 workstations with DEC AXP 21164 processors linked by 100-Mbit/s Fast Ethernet. Listed configuration is 128 Mbytes of memory and a 4-Gbyte disk per workstation; footnote 2 states that two workstations instead have 512 Mbytes. PVM handles message passing; a coordinating task farms particle-surface solves to workers and broadcasts updated solutions. Runs took place under normal time-sharing load.
machine_configurations.location: HTML Workstation Farm / Computer Description and Cost Estimation; Footnotes 1–2; derived PDF pp. 5 and 9

research.problem: Compute suspension flow resistance in creeping-flow Stokes problems, using a falling or rotating test sphere inside a concentrated suspension; the authors explicitly distinguish this configuration-dependent resistance from an intrinsic shear viscosity.
research.algorithm: Completed Double Layer Boundary Element Method (CDLBEM); particle-surface domain decomposition with block-Jacobi-like updates and relaxation 0.5; asynchronous updates of the potential when a worker finishes; PVM task farming. Each particle/container surface has 96 or 150 nine-node quadrilateral elements, Gaussian quadrature, and stated relative convergence thresholds of 1e-3 for the potential and velocity changes.
research.scientific_result: The calculated sedimentation response rises more sharply with particle concentration and varies more across configurations than the rotational response. The paper compares values with Thomas’ experimental bounds and empirical relations, and illustrates improved convergence from asynchronous updating for a 35% volume-fraction configuration.
research.location: HTML Formulation / Problem Description, CDLBEM and Domain Decomposition, Numerical Scheme; Results / Suspension Viscosities; derived PDF pp. 2–6

papers.title: N-body Simulation of Galaxy Formation on GRAPE-4 Special-Purpose Computer
papers.field: Computational astrophysics; high-resolution gravitational N-body simulation of galaxy formation
papers.summary: Fukushige and Makino follow the collapse of a cold-dark-matter density peak with direct gravitational interactions, fourth-order Hermite integration and individual hierarchical timesteps. GRAPE-4 pipelines calculate gravitational forces and their time derivatives while a DEC host integrates particle orbits. The calculation uses 786,400 particles to resolve the developing galaxy more finely; the audited author version reports a whole-run average application rate and a separate cost-per-performance estimate.

machine_configurations.name: GRAPE-4
machine_configurations.facility: University of Tokyo (authors’ affiliation; installation room not specified).
machine_configurations.configuration: The audited run uses three of the system’s four clusters. Each active cluster has a host-interface board, control board and nine processor boards. Each processor board has one PROMETHEUS predictor chip, particle-data memory and 48 physical HARP chips, with 47 used for calculation. There are 1,269 active HARP pipelines at 32 MHz. Each pipeline performs the author-counted 49 floating-point operations in three cycles. The paper’s 663 Gflops is theoretical peak, kept separate from the 332 Gflops run average.
machine_configurations.location: PDF pp. 3-4, Section 2 (GRAPE-4 System).

machine_configurations.name: DEC AXP 3900 host
machine_configurations.configuration: Host model named in the timing description. The host handles orbit integration and other work while GRAPE accelerates the pairwise gravitational force and first derivative. Processor count, host arithmetic precision, operating-system version and memory are not specified.

The numerator is 49 x N x n floating-point operations, where N = 786,400 and n is the number of individual steps. The authors count one square root or division as four operations.

The 2.8 billion years is modeled physical duration, not elapsed measurement time or the benchmark date.

papers.title: Economical High Performance Parallel Simulations of Wind Instruments
papers.field: Computational musical acoustics; compressible computational fluid dynamics
papers.summary: Skordos simulates the interaction of airflow and sound in wind instruments with an explicit lattice Boltzmann solver and a fourth-order stabilizing filter. Spatial subdomains run on a shared Ethernet cluster of HP workstations, with automatic migration when a host becomes busy. The paper derives an application FLOP rate and a dedicated-equipment performance/price estimate for the original-submission implementation; a newer communication-overlap efficiency is described separately.

machine_configurations.configuration: 20 active non-dedicated HP9000 workstations (models 715/50 and 712/60 are named), normally selected from 25 hosts to leave migration targets. Shared-bus Ethernet, HP-UX and TCP/IP; spatial subdomains exchange boundaries. The price example uses a model 712/60 with 16 MB RAM and network connection; about 6 MB is used for a 200 x 200 subregion.

measurements.measurement_method: The author counts 163 multiplication-equivalents plus 118 additions per fluid node per integration step. Division counts as one multiplication; byte copying/advection and communication add no FLOPs to the numerator. papers.field: Quantum molecular dynamics and electronic-structure simulation
papers.summary: A localized-orbital tight-binding method replaces global diagonalization with independent Chebyshev-recursion calculations. Sparse Hamiltonian operations and spatial truncation reduce the large-system work to linear scaling, while a coarse-grained PVM decomposition assigns atoms and their orbitals to workstations. Cache reuse, dot-product loops and hand-tuned multiply-add assembly improve node performance. The author report benchmarks liquid silicon and compares elapsed timestep cost with conventional diagonalization, keeping algorithmic work reduction separate from raw machine throughput.

machine_configurations.configuration: Eight HP 9000/735 RISC workstations linked by FDDI and programmed with PVM. A localized orbital and associated matrix data fit in a workstation 256K cache. Atoms are distributed across processors; each computes its local electronic orbitals and forces. The master also advances atom trajectories and broadcasts new positions. Exact CPU clock, RAM capacity, operating system, PVM/compiler versions and floating-point precision are not specified.

methods.description: Localized electronic orbitals are generated using a Chebyshev recursion dominated by sparse Hamiltonian-matrix/vector operations. An 8-angstrom truncation radius in the benchmark makes the asymptotic work linear in atom count. Two index arrays identify atoms inside localization regions and nonzero Hamiltonian elements. Dot products, loop unrolling by four and cache reuse improve irregular sparse operations; relevant assembly is hand-optimized to generate floating multiply-add instructions.

papers.title: 50 GFlops Molecular Dynamics on the Connection Machine 5
papers.field: Short-range molecular dynamics and atomistic materials simulation
papers.summary: SPaSM makes large atomistic materials simulations practical by dividing space into processor domains and smaller interaction cells. It exchanges particle data across domain boundaries, evaluates short-range forces on the CM-5 vector units, and caches cells in vector-accessible memory. The study compares interaction cutoffs and scaling, showing why a faster particle update can have a lower FLOP rate, and illustrates the method with an impact simulation.

machine_configurations.name: Connection Machine CM-5
machine_configurations.facility: The authors are affiliated with the Theoretical Division and Advanced Computing Laboratory, Los Alamos National Laboratory. The performance section identifies CM-5 partitions but does not individually identify a facility for every timing.
machine_configurations.configuration: Runs use 32–1,024 processing nodes, plus a 4-node scaling example. Each node has a SPARC processor, four vector units at a stated peak of 32 Mflops each, and four 8-Mbyte memory banks (32 Mbytes per node). Node memory is divided into SPARC and parallel-memory allocations. ANSI C calls CMMD explicitly; an approximately 60-line CDPEAC assembly kernel evaluates forces. The paper states 128 GFlops theoretical peak for a 1,024-node machine.
machine_configurations.location: Derived PDF pp. 2–4, sections 2–4; p. 6, section 5

research.problem: Integrate Newtonian dynamics for very large 3-D systems of particles with short-range interactions, aimed at defects, fracture and impact in materials.
research.workload: Lennard-Jones 6-12 pair potential with interaction cutoffs of 5 sigma and 2.5 sigma; all calculations double precision. The timing setup begins with a cubic lattice chosen to rearrange into an fcc configuration, so particles migrate across processors.
research.algorithm: Geometric domain decomposition; each processing node subdivides its region into cells just larger than the cutoff. An interaction path visits neighboring cells, exploiting Newton’s third law; CMMD exchanges cell data and asynchronously redistributes moved particles. Four vector units evaluate blocks of interactions. A FIFO cache of cells in parallel memory reduces repeated transfers from SPARC memory.
research.location: Derived PDF pp. 1–5; impact example pp. 6–8

papers.title: The Factorization of the Ninth Fermat Number
papers.field: Computational number theory and distributed integer factorization
papers.summary: A distributed number field sieve factors the ninth Fermat number using donated workstation cycles and a Connection Machine for the final linear algebra. The paper explains the arithmetic construction, relation collection, sparse-matrix reduction and verification of the resulting prime factors.
machines: Distributed DEC3100, SPARC and DEC SRC Firefly workstations
65536-processor Connection Machine at SCRI, Florida State University
Cray X-MP (final primality proof; no audited timing)

machine_configurations.name: Distributed workstation network
machine_configurations.facility: Bellcore, DEC SRC and volunteer institutions worldwide
machine_configurations.configuration: Started on about 35 Bellcore DEC3100/SPARC workstations; DEC SRC Firefly network joined in mid-March 1990. About 700 DEC3100 equivalents are estimated for donated work, not an exact simultaneous processor count.
machine_configurations.location: Printed pp. 339–340 / PDF sheets 11–12

machine_configurations.name: Connection Machine
machine_configurations.facility: Supercomputer Computation Research Institute, Florida State University
machine_configurations.configuration: 65536-processor machine; remote Gaussian elimination executed by Roger Frye and Mike McKenna of Thinking Machines. Machine model beyond Connection Machine is not specified in the audited paper.
machine_configurations.location: Printed p. 345 / PDF sheet 14

machine_configurations.name: DEC SRC matrix preprocessing and backup
machine_configurations.configuration: Fifteen workstations used to reconstruct factorizations/unit contributions; a four-processor Firefly supported backup elimination. Backup timing estimates are not treated as completed comparative benchmarks.
machine_configurations.location: Printed pp. 343–345 / PDF sheets 13–14

method.algorithm: Number field sieve specialized to F9=2^512+1, factoring its 148-digit cofactor after removal of the known factor 2424833; uses the number ring Z[2^(1/5)] and two-large-prime partial relations. Structured Gaussian elimination reduces the relation matrix before dense elimination modulo 2.
method.workload: 155-digit ninth Fermat number; newly found factors have 49 and 99 decimal digits. This completed computation is dated 15 June 1990; it is not a general random 155-digit-number factoring benchmark.
method.decomposition: Independent ranges of b values assigned to workstations; relations and completed-range reports sent by electronic mail to DEC SRC. Missing ranges were reassigned after approximately ten days. Relation cycles and matrix construction were centralized.
method.numerics: Factoring and F2 linear algebra use exact integer/finite-field relations; the text also discusses limited-precision logarithms for recovering unit exponents and logarithmic sieve heuristics. It gives no overall floating-point precision specification or FLOP-count method.
method.counting_and_timing: MIPS-years are explicitly estimated instruction equivalents. The three-hour duration is a reported matrix-stage run with no timer or complete I/O boundary specified. Primality of both factors was subsequently proved using a Cray X-MP Jacobi-sum implementation.

measurements.machine: Distributed workstation network (DEC3100, SPARC and DEC SRC Firefly participants)
measurements.precision: Integer factorization workload; floating-point precision is not a performance metric here. The estimate is in instruction equivalents; implementation word widths and exact use/precision of logarithmic sieving screens are not specified.
measurements.scope: Estimated computational effort for the sieving/relation-collection stage; not total factorization elapsed time and not FLOP/s.
measurements.scale: Approximately 2.2 million b values processed by 9 May 1990, each sieved over 10^8 a values. Authors estimate approximately 700 DEC3100 workstation equivalents, rather than claiming an audited physical host count.
measurements.measurement_method: Authors estimate host equivalents from completed work and mostly night-time donated cycles. They define 1 MIPS-year as approximately 3.15×10^13 instructions. No hardware instruction-counter protocol or exact CPU-time accounting is supplied.
measurements.location: PDF sheet 12, left / printed p. 340, §6 Sieving
measurements.measurement_date_context: Sieving began in mid-February 1990 and the reported 2.2-million-b milestone is dated 9 May 1990; the exact accounting interval for 340 MIPS-years is not separately dated.
measurements.conference_update_status: No authenticated later competition/presentation update established.
measurements.note: The same paragraph reports >3000 MIPS over five weeks as an estimate. These instruction measures are not converted to floating-point throughput or promoted to a prize score.

measurements.machine: 65536-processor Connection Machine at SCRI, Florida State University
measurements.precision: Exact arithmetic over the two-element field F2 / modulo 2 for Gaussian elimination; no floating-point precision applies. Physical bit/word packing details are not given.
measurements.scope: Reported duration of the successful dense Gaussian-elimination run only; not the whole factoring job or distributed sieving.
measurements.scale: Structured elimination first reduced a 226688×199203 sparse F2 matrix to a dense 72413×72213 matrix, called the 72000-matrix in the narrative; a few hundred row dependencies were produced.
measurements.measurement_method: Narrative reports three hours for a first solve followed by an output-routine crash and another three hours for the successful second run. papers.title: Performance of A Supernodal General Sparse Solver on the CRAY Y-MP: 1.68 GFLOPS with Autotasking
papers.field: Sparse numerical linear algebra for structural analysis and scientific simulation
papers.summary: A production sparse solver groups columns with shared sparsity patterns into supernodes to reduce indirect memory traffic and preserve vector performance. Tuned matrix-vector kernels then use Cray microtasking and autotasking. Experiments separate real structural matrices from constructed three-dimensional model problems and show where limited supernode size restricts parallel gains.

method.algorithm: Supernodal sparse factorization: columns with essentially common sparsity patterns are grouped, replacing separate gather-SAXPY-scatter operations with gather/multiple-SAXPY/scatter updates implemented as tuned matrix-vector multiplication.
method.parallelization: Two costly matrix-vector kernels with indexed addressing are microtasked/autotasked by row strips. Runtime switch-over points choose sequential or parallel kernels according to supernode shape; preserving vectorization and tuning these thresholds are central.
method.implementation: Production package developed by Boeing Computer Services researchers and available from Cray Research. Table 1 compares assembly SGEMVS+SGMVIS, unrolled Fortran SGEMV8+SGMVI8 and inline Fortran implementations.
method.workloads: Sixteen matrix cases are tabulated: Boeing-Harwell structural problems, NASA Langley structural matrices and synthetic CUBE10/15/17 models. CUBE17 is not relabelled as a physical finite-element result.
method.counting_and_timing: MFLOPS and factorization timing are reported, but no FLOP-count equation, profiler/counter protocol, timer name or overall arithmetic precision is supplied. Hardware peak, projected 6.0 ns clock improvement and kernel-stage rates are kept separate from application claims.
